fields.features_heading: What Emergent Builds Into a Vocabulary Quiz
fields.features_subheading: A vocabulary quiz tests whether a reader knows what words mean. Emergent builds the quiz and its scoring, and the table behind it.
fields.feature_1:
Questions written from your word list

Paste the week's words and Emergent writes one question per word, with the right meaning and three wrong ones of the same kind. A follow-up prompt changes any question you dislike.
fields.feature_2:
A score and a meaning at the end

Students see their score and a result line when they finish, then every word with its meaning and an example sentence. You choose the score bands, such as 0 to 3 out of 8.
fields.feature_3:
Every answer in a database you own

Each answer is saved as a row in a database you own, with the student, the word, the choice, and the date. Sort by word to see what a class missed, or by student to plan retakes.
fields.feature_4:
One question per screen on a phone

Students and adult learners answer one question per screen on a phone, with a progress bar on top. A 12-word quiz fits into the last few minutes on the bus before a class starts.
fields.feature_5:
Retake links and parent emails

Set a pass mark, and anyone below it can be sent a retake by email. Parents can get a score email on Sundays, and a tutor can get a list of the students ready for new words.
fields.feature_6:
Your own domain, and the code on GitHub

Put the quiz on your school's own domain, included in Emergent and billed in credits. On paid plans, export the full code to your GitHub repository and run it again next year.

fields.usecase_heading: How Four Teachers Run a Vocabulary Quiz
fields.tab_content_1:
Reluctant, which 47 students missed, returns Friday

Each Monday, 84 students across 3 English classes at Halvard Middle School take a 10-word quiz. Each answer is saved with the student's name and the word. By Thursday, 47 of 84 had missed reluctant, the most of any word, and it went first on Friday's review list.
fields.tab_content_2:
A retake link for the 9 who scored under 14

Crestmoor High's Spanish 2 class of 31 takes a 20-word food quiz that matches each Spanish word to its English meaning. Anyone who scores under 14 of 20 gets a retake link by email the next morning. After the first round, 9 of 31 got one, and the retake asks the same 20 words in a new order.
fields.tab_content_3:
Parents see each week's score every Sunday

Larchmont Test Prep sends each student 15 words a week from its 300-word SAT list. Every Sunday, a parent email shows that week's score beside the 3 weeks before it. Owen Lindqvist's email read 9, 11, 13, and 14 of 15, and his tutor started him on the next list a week early.
fields.tab_content_4:
Invoice opens the next class after 9 of 22 miss it

A class of 22 adults meets on Tuesday evenings at the Pinecrest Library to learn English. Before each class, they take a 12-word workplace quiz on their phones, one question per screen. Last week, 9 of 22 missed invoice, more than any other word, and the teacher opened the next class with it.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Vocabulary Quiz
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to create a vocabulary quiz that tests real word knowledge and shows which words to teach again.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Pick words from this week's reading
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Put some words inside a sentence
fields.howto_step_1_des: Choose words students met in this week's reading or unit, not a random list. A weekly quiz of about 10 words fits in 10 minutes of class. Paste the list into your prompt, and Emergent drafts one question for each word.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Write the correct meaning in plain words a student would use, then check it against a dictionary. Keep it short enough to read at a glance. If the right answer is much longer than the others, students learn to pick the longest option.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Give each question three wrong meanings of the same kind and length as the right one. If the word is an adjective, every option should describe something. Leave out joke options and "all of the above", which give the answer away.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Ask a few questions with the word inside a sentence, such as "She kept a tenacious grip on the rope." A sentence checks whether a student can read the word in use, not only recall a definition. Mix both kinds in one quiz.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Set the score bands and messages
fields.howto_step_5_des: Decide what each score means before anyone takes the quiz, such as 0 to 3, 4 to 6, and 7 to 8 out of 8. Write one line for each band that says what to do next, like reviewing the missed words that evening.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Test it on two students first
fields.howto_step_6_des: Have 2 students, or a colleague, take the quiz before the class does. Watch for a question with two defensible answers and for a wrong option nobody picks. Fix both, then open the quiz to the whole class.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Reteach the words missed the most
fields.howto_step_7_des: After the quiz closes, sort the answers by word. Start the next lesson with the 2 or 3 words missed the most, use each one in a new sentence, and put them back on next week's quiz to see whether they stuck.

faq_plan.a: A vocabulary quiz is a short test of whether you know what words mean. Each question gives a word, alone or inside a sentence, and asks you to pick its meaning from a few options. The score shows which words you know and which ones to study again.

faq_plan.q: How to create a vocabulary quiz?
faq_plan.ref: how to create a vocabulary quiz
faq_plan.a: Start with about 10 words from what your students are reading, write the correct meaning for each, and add three believable wrong ones. With Emergent's AI survey builder, you paste the list into a prompt and get a working quiz that scores every answer and saves it to a database you own.

faq_plan.q: How to make a good vocabulary quiz for adults?
faq_plan.ref: how to make a good vocabulary quiz
faq_plan.a: A good vocabulary quiz for adults uses words from their work or daily reading, offers wrong options that look as likely as the right one, and asks some words inside a sentence. Show the meaning after each answer to turn a miss into a lesson. Keep it short enough to finish on a phone during a break.

faq_plan.q: How to make a matching vocabulary quiz?
faq_plan.ref: how to make a matching vocabulary quiz
faq_plan.a: To make a matching vocabulary quiz, list the words in one column and their meanings in another, shuffled, and ask students to pair each word with its meaning. Add one or two extra meanings that match no word; then the last pair is never a free point. Keep each set to about 10 pairs.

faq_plan.q: How to make a vocabulary quiz online?
faq_plan.ref: how to make a vocabulary quiz online
faq_plan.a: To make a vocabulary quiz online, use a quiz builder that scores the answers for you and keeps the results. Type each word with its meaning and three wrong options, set a pass mark, and share the link. On Emergent, there is no cap on how many students take the quiz, and each result is a row you can sort by word.

faq_plan.q: How to make a vocabulary quiz with definitions?
faq_plan.ref: how to make a vocabulary quiz with definiton
faq_plan.a: Write each word's definition in plain language first, then ask in both directions: show the word and ask for its definition, or show the definition and ask for the word. Check every definition against a dictionary before you publish, and show it again on the results screen with an example sentence.

faq_plan.q: How to make an SAT vocabulary quiz app?
faq_plan.ref: how to make vocabulary quiz app
faq_plan.a: To make an SAT vocabulary quiz app, decide what it must do beyond one quiz, such as weekly word lists, scores over time, and retake rules. On Emergent, you describe that in a prompt and get the app with its database, and a follow-up prompt adds parent emails later.

faq_plan.q: What should a vocabulary quiz maker include?
faq_plan.a: A vocabulary quiz maker should include scoring for each answer, the right meaning after it, and results kept by word and by student. Results by word tell you what to reteach. Results by student tell you who needs a retake.

faq_plan.q: Can a vocabulary quiz generator create the wrong answers?
faq_plan.a: Yes, a vocabulary quiz generator can create three wrong meanings for each word, but read every one before the quiz goes out. A wrong option that is also a correct meaning of the word, or one far shorter than the rest, lets students guess their way to points.

faq_plan.q: How do you make a Spanish vocabulary quiz?
faq_plan.a: Build a Spanish vocabulary quiz around one theme, such as food or the classroom, and ask in both directions: Spanish word to English meaning, then English to Spanish. Write each noun with its article, the way students will need to say it, and mix the two directions in one round.

quiz.title: Vocabulary Quiz: 8 Words, How Many Do You Know?
quiz.intro: Eight questions on everyday words that show up in books, news, and class. Pick one answer per question; your score and the meanings show at the end.

questions.text: A flower that blooms for a single morning could be called ephemeral. What does ephemeral mean?
questions.explanation: Ephemeral describes anything that does not last: a pop-up shop, a snowman, a trend that fades in a week.

source.quote: Something that is fleeting or short-lived is ephemeral

questions.text: A friend gives you a candid opinion of your essay. What kind of opinion is it?
questions.explanation: A candid answer says what the speaker really thinks, even when the listener would rather hear praise.

source.quote: Straightforward and truthful talk might be described with the adjective candid

questions.text: Which phrase describes a frugal person?
questions.explanation: Frugal is about careful spending, such as buying clothes secondhand. It is a kinder word than cheap.

source.quote: A person who lives simply and economically can be called frugal

questions.text: What does tenacious mean in the sentence "She kept a tenacious grip on the rope"?

options.text: Not easily letting go or giving up

questions.explanation: Tenacious comes up for grips and for people. A tenacious student keeps working on a problem until it gives way.

source.quote: not easily letting go or giving up

questions.text: A headline can be read two different ways. Which word describes it?
questions.explanation: Something ambiguous is open to more than one interpretation, so the reader has to guess which meaning was intended.

source.quote: Look to the adjective ambiguous when you need to describe something that's open to more than one interpretation

questions.text: A neighbor shovels snow for the whole street. Which phrase explains why that is benevolent?

options.text: Does good deeds or shows goodwill

questions.explanation: Benevolent fits kindness offered freely, like clearing a path nobody asked for.

source.quote: for someone who does good deeds or shows goodwill

questions.text: Phones seem to be in every pocket and on every table. Which word fits that idea?
questions.explanation: Ubiquitous means present in all places at the same time, or close enough that it feels that way.

source.quote: present in all places at the same time, reach for the adjective ubiquitous

questions.text: A teacher calls a book report verbose. What is the report doing?
questions.explanation: A verbose report uses far more words than it needs. Cutting it in half makes the point easier to find.

source.quote: A verbose book report goes on and on

results.title: Keep Building Your Word Bank
results.description: A few of these words were new to you, and that is the point of a quiz. Open the answers below, read each example sentence, and try the quiz again tomorrow to see which words stuck.

results.title: Your Range Is Growing
results.description: You knew most of the everyday words. Check the answers below for the ones that slipped, then use each of them in a sentence of your own this week.

results.title: Ready for Harder Words
results.description: You matched almost every word to its meaning. Try a harder list next, with words like laconic, obstinate, and gregarious.
